extracted.intended_audience: owners/operators of combustion-turbine electric generating units (EGUs), state and federal regulators, industry stakeholders, and environmental/legal advisors
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the standards, performance metrics, and evaluative criteria the EPA used to define the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) and numeric New Source Performance Standards (NSPS) for base, intermediate, and low load combustion-turbine EGUs, including phase-1 (efficient generation + O&M) and phase-2 (CCS) components.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER phase-1 for base load combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of highly efficient combined cycle technology in combination with best operating and maintenance (O&M) practices for base load EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA concludes this combination supports a numeric standard of performance representing best-performing EGUs in the subcategory. Finalized large base load standard (phase-1) is 800 lb CO2/MWh-gross for units with base load heat input > 2,000 MMBtu/h. Basis: long-term demonstrated performance, normalization for configuration and cooling, and estimation of achievable rates at lower capacity factors. Considerations include cooling technology, multi-shaft vs single-shaft design, duty cycle, and long-term degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER phase-1 for small base load combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of highly efficient combined cycle technology in combination with best O&M practices for small base load EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finalized phase-1 standard for small base load turbines (those with base load rating of 250 MMBtu/h) is 900 lb CO2/MWh-gross. EPA based this on demonstrated long-term data (e.g., Holland Energy Park) and adjustment for possible improved technologies (e.g., supercritical CO2 HRSG) and normalization assumptions (cooling, configuration, capacity factor).

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER phase-1 for intermediate load combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the most efficient available simple cycle technology in combination with best O&M practices for intermediate (variable) load EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA finalized an intermediate-load standard of 1,170 lb CO2/MWh-gross. Rationale: review of 12-month demonstrated emission rates for simple cycle turbines since 2015, technological variations (aeroderivative vs frame; water injection vs dry low NOx), and the need to preserve options (e.g., avoiding a standard that effectively requires intercooling or water injection for most units).

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER phase-1 for low load combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of lower-emitting fuels qualifies as the BSER for low load combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA proposed standards ranging from 120 to 160 lb CO2/MMBtu depending on the fuel burned. (Standards expressed on a heat-input basis for low-load EGUs; compliance timing and averaging consistent with other subcategories.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-2 BSER for base load combustion turbines (CCS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) achieving 90 percent capture of emitting CO2 as the second component of BSER for base load combustion turbines, effective beginning in 2035.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA used a 90% capture assumption (and reduced the emissions rate by 89% in calculations) assuming CCS is operational anytime the turbine is operating. EPA solicited comments on 75–90% range but determined 90% demonstrated and appropriate. Standards adjusted for fuels other than natural gas (e.g., 100% distillate oil example yields 120 lb CO2/MWh-gross). Eligibility for IRC section 45Q tax credits (existing EGU criterion of 75% equivalent capture) informed conclusions about partial capture economics.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12-operating-month rolling average compliance metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Emission standards apply at all times and compliance is determined on a 12-operating-month rolling average basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA calculates the 12-month CO2 emission rate by dividing the sum of CO2 emissions by the sum of gross electrical energy output over the same 12-operating-month period. Agency prefers long-term averages (12-month) for never-to-exceed NSPS because they capture degradation and variable operating conditions. Commenters generally supported the 12-month rolling average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of long-term demonstrated emission data to set achievable standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards should be based on long-term (12-month) demonstrated emission rates rather than short-term high-performance data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term averages account for degradation, variable conditions, and operating variability. EPA used data from 2015–2023 CEMS submissions, sorted by lowest maximum 12-operating-month emissions rate per unit, to identify achievable lb CO2/MWh-gross values. This avoids relying on short-term or ideal-condition demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for duty cycle / capacity factor in setting standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards must account for emissions variation by operating load; emission rates are lowest at roughly 80–90% load and increase at lower loads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA binned hourly data by load and season to isolate duty cycle and temperature effects. To address potential compliance issues at lower duty cycles, EPA estimated emissions at a 40% 12-operating-month capacity factor for best-performing units using trends in emission rate vs capacity factor, and used that to set achievable standards for units operating at lower percent of potential electric sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for ambient temperature impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the effect of ambient temperature/season on emission rates and whether regional variation is material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA compared emissions at similar loads across seasons and found minimal differences (single digits; <1% for combined cycle EGUs). Conclusion: ambient temperature has minimal impact relative to duty cycle; mitigation (inlet cooling or Rankine cycle generation) reduces temperature impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization adjustments for cooling technology and turbine configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust demonstrated emission rates to account for differences in cooling technology (wet vs dry) and combined cycle configuration (multi-shaft 2/3-on-1 vs single-shaft 1-on-1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA increased reported emissions rates for units with cooling towers by 1.0% to represent potential new units using dry cooling. EPA increased emissions of 2-1 and 3-1 combined cycle turbines by 1.4% to account for potential new units using a 1-1 configuration. EPA also adjusted demonstrated rates to estimate emissions at lower capacity factors. These normalizations create a more conservative, broadly-applicable standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing nationwide standards on atypical outlier facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not set national standards strictly on performance of uniquely configured or unrepresentative units (e.g., multi-shaft units, special cooling, or very large aeroderivative simple cycles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA rejected use of the Okeechobee Clean Energy Center (3-on-1, recirculating cooling, high-duty-cycle new unit) and Scattergood (very large aeroderivative simple cycles with water injection) as sole bases for nationwide standards because they are not representative of typical design choices, cooling constraints, size ranges, or long-term degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of fuels other than natural gas for deriving source-specific standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners/operators burning fuels other than natural gas may elect to determine a source-specific standard by scaling natural gas-based standards by the ratio of the heat input-based emissions rates of the specific fuel(s) to natural gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA gives example: for a large base load combustion turbine burning 100% distillate oil during the 12-operating-month period, the NSPS emissions rate would be 1,070 lb CO2/MWh-gross (based on the ratio approach). For phase-2 (CCS) standards, EPA similarly adjusts for uncontrolled emission differences across fuels (example: 100% distillate oil CCS-based rate = 120 lb CO2/MWh-gross).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of operational realities raised by commenters (start/stop, backup fuel, degradation, duct burners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards and compliance regimes must consider practical operating conditions such as cycling, backup fuel use, degradation, and potential differences in startup/shutdown timing between turbine and CCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters requested account for start/stop cycles, backup fuel use, degradation, and compliance tolerance. EPA addressed some by relying on 12-month averaging and long-term data; solicited comment about CCS availability/reliability vs turbine and potential uncontrolled periods. EPA considered but did not accept some suggested exclusions (e.g., duct burners), instead using long-term demonstrated data and normalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic/financial viability consideration for CCS (tax credit and partial capture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of CCS as BSER must consider economic incentives such as IRC section 45Q tax credit eligibility thresholds and how partial capture affects economics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA noted IRC 45Q eligibility for existing EGUs requires design capture rates equivalent to 75% of a baseline emission rate by mass. Partial capture below this threshold would not receive the tax credit and thus could be too expensive to qualify as BSER. Even partial capture meeting threshold yields lower credits when capture fraction is lower, affecting cost-effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of CHP as BSER due to thermal-host and siting constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Combined Heat and Power (CHP) not selected as BSER because CHP requires primary thermal output to a proximate thermal host with consistent, large thermal demand and hence is limited geographically and in scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explained CHP's constraints: thermal hosts with sufficient demand (refining, chemical, pulp/paper, food processing, district energy) generally only support smaller EGUs (several hundred MW max), limited geographic locations, reliance on continued host operation increases financing risk, potential need to discount thermal pricing, and difficulty in finding suitably sized hosts—therefore EPA did not propose CHP as BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of hybrid power plants as BSER due to cost-effectiveness and resource constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrid power plants (e.g., solar thermal integrated with fossil-fired EGUs) are not included in BSER because of knowledge gaps on costs and concerns about cost-effectiveness and geographic/resource limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cited modest CO2 reductions from realistic integration (example: solar thermal sized to 10% max steam turbine output producing ~3% of annual generation and ~3% reduction in CO2 with ~1% LCOE increase), need for abundant sunshine and land (DNI limitations), steam-turbine oversizing causing reduced efficiency at non-solar times, and NREL's analysis indicating solar augmentation often not cost-effective. Commenters provided no new cost-effective data; EPA excluded hybrids from BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstructed stationary combustion turbine upgrade eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconstructed combustion turbines can use upgrade packages and retrofits (e.g., Advanced Gas Path, Hot Start on the Fly, compressor restaging, HRSG additions, steam injection) to meet applicable standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA noted manufacturers sell performance/efficiency upgrade packages that increase output and efficiency; examples: GE Advanced Gas Path, Siemens Hot Start on the Fly, Solar compressor restaging. Steam injection retrofit estimated at ~$250/kW and can be up to 60% smaller than equivalent HRSG for retrofit. Conversions from simple cycle to combined cycle via HRSG additions have been performed (e.g., Riverton Unit 12, Energy Center Dover). Such options can enable reconstructed units to comply with intermediate-load standards or convert to combined cycle to meet base-load standards.
